newsitem.title: FINLAND: BANK OF FINLAND SEES SLOW INFLATION, MODERATE RATES.
newsitem.headline: BANK OF FINLAND SEES SLOW INFLATION, MODERATE RATES.

text.p: The Bank of Finland said on Wednesday in its Markka & Talous publication that inflation looked set to remain calm over the next few years and that this would help keep the interest rate trend moderate.
"The conditions for inflation to remain calm over the next few years are very favourable, in line with earlier expectations," the Bank of Finland said.
"This, in turn, promotes keeping the interest rate trend moderate," it said.

Speaking at a news conference, Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen, referring to the central bank's key monetary policy tool, the tender rate, said: "At the moment there are no pressures in either direction."
The tender rate has been unchanged at 3.00 percent since October 9.
In Markka & Talous, the central bank said Finnish underlying inflation would be "slightly below 2 percent" in 1997.
This year, the rise in headline CPI would be around one percent, it said.
In October, the year-on-year CPI rise was 0.7 percent. Core inflation data, lagging one month behind, showed a year-on-year increase of 0.1 percent in September.
The central bank's target is for a core inflation rate around no more than about two percent.
"Despite the strengthening of domestic demand inflation expectations have remained moderate," the Bank of Finland said.
Finnish economic growth this year had been based largely on a recovery in private consumption, the central bank said.

"Consumer confidence in the economy has strengthened which indicates that the growth in consumption will continue," it said, adding lower interest rates had led to a pick-up in household credit demand.

"According to three-month interest rate forwards, interest rate expectations for next year are moderate," the Bank of Finland said. According to FRA (forward rate agreement) quotations, the three-month Helibor interest rate is seen in a 3.2-3.8 percent range next year. It was 3.09 percent on Tuesday.

The fall in Finnish long-term interest rates came to an end in mid-October with the 10-year bond yield spread over German Bunds narrowing to below 50 basis points. The yield gap widened slightly in November, the central bank said.
The current gap "reflects the view that Finland aims to be among the first in EMU," Hamalainen told the news conference.
On Wednesday morning, the 10-year yield gap was 59 basis points.
In Markka & Talous, the central bank said Finland's current account surplus would remain big until the end of this year, but the full-year surplus would fall slightly short of last year's.
"This year, exports of forest industry products may be slightly smaller than forecast," the Bank of Finland said.
"The fall in export prices of paper may go on for a longer time than expected," it said.
"The terms of trade may also weaken more than expected and so the current account surplus is not expected to grow this year quite to the size of last year's," it said.
In 1995, the C/A surplus was 25 billion markka. In January-October this year the surplus was 15.4 billion markka, according to preliminary central bank data.
The Bank of Finland said the Finnish economy was expected to develop favourably in the next few years and conditions to balance the state finances were good.
Finland would reach the Maastricht criterion of a public sector deficit below three percent of GDP already this year, it said, adding the current account would remain in surplus.
"The slow fall in unemployment will continue," it said.

Hamalainen told the news conference that due to the still high unemployment she saw no fears for an overheating of the economy. The ongoing rise in apartment prices was not expected to raise inflation expectations, the central bank said.
--Peter Starck, Helsinki Newsroom +358 - 9 - 680 50 245
